terms.gloss: hold back, restrain, keep in check
evidence: Ter. Haut. 919: nōn tū tē cohibēs?
Cic. Off. 2.18: mōtūs animī perturbātōs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of feelings, hands, oneself: īrās cohibēre (Verg. A. 12.314, Lewis & Short); ab aliēnō cohibēre manūs, keep one’s hands off other people’s things (Plaut. Trin. 1019).

evidence: Tac. Agr. 4.4: nī prūdentia mātris incēnsum ac flagrantem animum coercuisset
terms.comment: Of keeping people, animals or passions within bounds, by force if need be.

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; with the dative, or ā and the ablative
terms.comment: Sibi temperāre, to control oneself (Caes. BG 1.33, Lewis & Short); īrae temperāre, to keep one’s anger in check (Liv. 33.20.7, Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, deponent; with the dative
evidence: Plaut. Mil. 1215: moderāre animō, nē sīs cupidus
Hor. Ep. 1.2.59: quī nōn moderābitur īrae (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Inv. 2.164: continentia est, per quam cupiditās cōnsiliī gubernātiōne regitur (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To lose control is nōn esse apud sē, to be beside oneself (Ter. Haut. 920–921).

terms.register: mostly poetic and post-Augustan; not in Cicero (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: nōn tū tē cohibēs? nōn tē respicis? … — prae īrācundiā, Menedēme, nōn sum apud mē.
phrases.english: Won’t you control yourself? Won’t you think of yourself? … — I’m so angry, Menedemus, I’m beside myself.

phrases.latin: īra furor brevis est; animum rege, quī nisi pāret, imperat
phrases.english: anger is a short madness: control your temper, for unless it obeys, it gives the orders
